newsitem.title: UK: Debt markets set to sprint ahead on U.S. election.
newsitem.headline: Debt markets set to sprint ahead on U.S. election.

text.p: By Jacqueline Thorpe,
Global debt markets were set to charge ahead on Wednesday, spurred on by a strong Treasuries market as U.S. presidential elections maintained the status quo in U.S. politics, analysts said.

Barring a bombshell victory by Republican candidate Bob Dole, the elections gave bond markets the best they could have hoped for -- a Democrat in the White House but Republicans in control of the Senate and set to take the House of Representatives, they said.
"The fact that we're not getting a major fiscal risk in the U.S. is good for all bond markets," said Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International in London.
"Inevitably Europe will be dragged higher by the sharp rally we've seen overnight," he said.

Stephen Hannah, head of research at IBJ International in London, added, "On the U.S. side if the market can fall below 6.5 percent on the long bond it may make a stab at 6.0 percent and that will pull up the other markets."
"That's a fairly important barrier but I don't sense at the moment investors are likely to weigh in with heavy profit taking," he said.

The bellwether long bond was quoted at 102-15 at 0748 GMT, yielding 6.559 percent, up from 102-04 at the New York finish on Tuesday. December T-bond futures were quoted at 114-09, up 16/32 in automated trade from the Chicago settlement.
Treasuries pushed ahead against German government bonds, squeezing the yield gap between 10-year bonds to 42 basis points from 46 at the close of European trade on Tuesday.
In Europe, December Bund futures on LIFFE were quoted at 100.35, up 24 basis points.
Gilts were higher too, quoted up 10/32 at 109-20.

By 0645 GMT, results showed Democratic President Bill Clinton routed Republican Bob Dole in the race for the White House with television networks projecting Clinton taking at least 30 of the 50 U.S. states.
The Republicans maintained control of the Senate. Both ABC and CNN television projected they would also take the House of Respersentatives once all results were in.

Chester said there may be some profit taking with the election result widely expected, but Hannah at IBJ noted the wall of Japanese money that has been supporting bond markets is not likely to disappear any time soon.
While U.S. Treasuries were well-supported to move ahead, European markets would now focus on other issues, namely European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), analysts said.
Hannah said this would likely lead core European debt to lag Treasuries.

"Certainly core Europe will probably underperform, partly because the political limelight has shifted away from the U.S. presidential race and to the political shenanigans of European monetary union," Hannah said.
Bunds, and bonds linked closely to the German market like Austrian and French debt, would suffer while Italian, Spanish and other high yielding debt would gain, he said.
Stuart Thomson, chief international economist at Nikko Europe here, agreed the main focus for bond investors would now be on Europe.
The next meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on November 13 was likely to be a non-event as markets expect interest rates to stay steady.

He said Greenspan has achieved a "soft-landing" in the economy. While it was reasonable to expect a buoyant Christmas sales period as a result of higher earnings in the U.S., data show spenders have been restrained so far.
"In essence what the electorate have voted for is Greenspan and his exceptional record which has placed Clinton in a position of power," he said.
